```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(OncoCohortSelect)
```

OncoCohortSelect helps to choose one of several single-arm cohorts studied in
parallel, for example combination regimens in the cohorts of a phase 2 trial,
with several efficacy and safety endpoints. The cohorts are compared by two
approaches:

* a posterior benefit-risk score (Chakraborty et al., 2026), computed for each
  cohort against target values or for a cohort relative to a reference cohort,
  and
* generalized pairwise comparisons of prioritized endpoints (Buyse, 2010),
  which give the net treatment benefit, the win ratio and the win odds of a
  cohort against a reference cohort.

The same functions analyze the data of a completed trial and of simulated
trials, so that a decision rule can be evaluated by simulation before the
trial and applied to its data afterwards.

## A first example

`SimCohorts()` simulates cohorts with correlated progression-free survival
(PFS), overall survival (OS) and objective response, generated by the
CorOncoEndpoints package, and an adverse event. Here one trial with two
cohorts of 50 patients is analyzed at month 24.

```{r}
arms <- list(
  Cohort1 = CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.4,
                                      death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 15),
  Cohort2 = CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = 8, orr = 0.45, resp.cor = 0.4,
                                      death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 18))
d <- SimCohorts(nsim = 1, n = c(50, 50), arms = arms, ae.rate = c(0.20, 0.35),
                cutoff = 24, a.time = c(0, 12), seed = 1)
head(d)
```

Endpoints are defined by the columns that hold them and by their favorable
direction; any number of binary and time-to-event endpoints can be used.

```{r}
eps <- list(
  Endpoint("OS", "tte", time = "os_tte", event = "os_event"),
  Endpoint("PFS", "tte", time = "pfs_tte", event = "pfs_event"),
  Endpoint("ORR", "binary", var = "response"),
  Endpoint("AE", "binary", var = "ae", higher.better = FALSE))
```

The benefit-risk score of each cohort against target values combines the
posterior probabilities that the response rate is at least 0.3, that the PFS
and OS probabilities at months 6 and 12 are at least 0.5 and 0.6, and that the
adverse event rate is at most 0.3.

```{r}
crit <- data.frame(endpoint = c("ORR", "PFS", "OS", "AE"),
                   target = c(0.30, 0.50, 0.60, 0.30), time = c(NA, 6, 12, NA))
BenefitRisk(d, eps, crit)
```

The pairwise comparisons of Cohort2 against Cohort1 use the priority order OS,
PFS, response and adverse event.

```{r}
w <- WinStat(d, eps, treatment = "Cohort2", control = "Cohort1")
w$ci
```

The net treatment benefit of Cohort2 is `r round(w$estimate[["ntb"]], 2)` and
its win ratio `r round(w$estimate[["wr"]], 2)`.

## Where to go next

* *Posterior benefit-risk score*: the models, the components against target
  values and relative to a reference cohort, weights and admissibility.
* *Net benefit and win ratio*: priority, thresholds, the scoring rules of
  Gehan and of Péron, and the confidence intervals.
* *Evaluating decision rules by simulation*: selecting one of three cohorts
  and comparing rules at a common probability of a false selection.
* *Analyzing a completed trial*: data in the style of ADaM data sets and the
  decision at the end of the trial.

## References

Buyse, M. (2010). Generalized pairwise comparisons of prioritized outcomes in
the two-sample problem. *Statistics in Medicine*, 29, 3245-3257.
https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.3923

Chakraborty, S., Dubey, A. K., Kumar, A. and Chan, I. (2026). A two-stage dose
optimization framework for oncology drug development with multiple efficacy
and safety endpoints via an integrated benefit-risk assessment. *Statistics in
Biopharmaceutical Research*, published online.
https://doi.org/10.1080/19466315.2026.2668381
